name: The Definition of Art
statement: What makes something a work of art, and whether art can be defined at all.
statementAccent: whether art can be defined at all
meaning: The definition of art is the problem of stating what art is: giving necessary and sufficient conditions for something to be a work of art, or otherwise explaining what unifies the diverse things we call art. It is one of the central problems of aesthetics. Traditional, classical definitions each singled out a feature: mimetic or representational theories, going back to Plato and Aristotle, held that art is imitation or representation, but this failed to cover abstract and non-representational art; expression theories, associated with Tolstoy and Collingwood, held that art is the expression of emotion; and formalism, associated with Clive Bell, held that art is significant form. Each was challenged by counterexamples, especially the twentieth-century avant-garde, above all Marcel Duchamp's readymades, such as Fountain, a urinal submitted as art in 1917. In 1956 Morris Weitz, in The Role of Theory in Aesthetics, drew on Wittgenstein's notion of family resemblance to argue that art cannot be defined at all: art is an open concept with no set of necessary and sufficient conditions, only overlapping resemblances, and creative art constantly expands it, so any closing definition would stifle creativity. Definitions after Weitz responded in various ways: the institutional theory of George Dickie, drawing on Arthur Danto's artworld, defines art relationally; Jerrold Levinson's historical definition ties art to prior artworks; Beardsley's functional definition ties it to aesthetic experience; and Berys Gaut offers a cluster account with no necessary conditions.
mechanism: The project of defining art proceeds by proposing conditions and testing them against the full range of things we count, and refuse to count, as art. Classical definitions each fastened on one manifest, exhibited property. The mimetic theory made representation essential, which fit painting and drama but excluded abstract painting and much music; the expression theory made the communication or clarification of emotion essential; formalism made significant form, the arrangement of lines and colors, essential. The decisive pressure on all such definitions came from radical modern art, especially Duchamp's readymades and later conceptual art, which are art yet share no common exhibited feature with traditional works and may even lack aesthetic interest by design. Weitz turned this into a general argument: since art is an open concept, endlessly extended by creative innovation, no fixed set of necessary and sufficient conditions can capture it, and the proper task of aesthetics is to describe family resemblances rather than to define. The definitions that followed accept that manifest properties will not do and look elsewhere. Relational definitions locate arthood not in what a work looks like but in its relations to a practice: the institutional theory holds that an object is art when it is an artifact on which someone acting on behalf of the artworld has conferred the status of candidate for appreciation. Historical definitions, such as Levinson's, hold that something is art when it is intended for regard in the ways prior artworks were correctly regarded. Functional definitions, such as Beardsley's, hold that art is made with the intention to afford an experience of marked aesthetic character. Cluster accounts, such as Gaut's, list many criteria, none necessary but jointly sufficient in various combinations.

examples.text: Mimetic, expression, and formalist definitions were each broken by modern art, above all Duchamp's readymade Fountain of 1917.
Weitz argued in 1956 that art is an open concept with no necessary and sufficient conditions, only family resemblances.
The institutional and historical definitions locate arthood in relations to the artworld or to prior art, not in manifest features.

variants.name: Anti-essentialism
variants.text: Weitz's view, drawing on Wittgenstein, that art is an open concept that cannot be defined by necessary and sufficient conditions.

variants.name: Post-Weitz definitions
variants.text: Institutional, historical, functional, and cluster accounts that respond to the anti-essentialist challenge.

whyItMatters: The definition of art is a foundational and enduring problem of aesthetics, and it became especially urgent in the twentieth century as art itself grew radically diverse. Once artists could exhibit a urinal, a stack of Brillo boxes, or a purely conceptual gesture as art, the question of what, if anything, unites all art, and of how to tell art from non-art, could no longer be answered by pointing to beauty, representation, or form. Weitz's anti-essentialist challenge, that art is an open concept resisting definition, reframed the whole field and forced defenders of definition to look beyond a work's visible properties to its place in a history and an institution, giving rise to the institutional, historical, and functional definitions that dominate the modern debate. The problem bears directly on practical questions, such as what belongs in museums, what deserves the attention and funding accorded to art, and how to make sense of conceptual and avant-garde work. It also connects to deep issues about concepts, essences, and family resemblance, and about the relation between art and aesthetic experience. Whether art can or should be defined remains genuinely open.

working.text: offer necessary and sufficient conditions, or a feature, that all and only artworks share.
check the proposal against abstract, conceptual, and readymade art that breaks classical definitions.
if manifest features fail, define art by relations to the artworld or prior art, or by a cluster of criteria.

limits: The definition of art remains unresolved, and the anti-essentialist challenge that it cannot be defined at all is still a live option. Every classical definition, mimetic, expressive, and formalist, was refuted by counterexamples from modern and avant-garde art, and Weitz's argument that art is an open concept, endlessly extended by creativity, casts doubt on the whole enterprise of definition. The definitions offered in response each face objections: the institutional theory is charged with circularity, since it uses the artworld to define art, and with failing to say what makes conferral appropriate; historical definitions must handle the very first art, which had no predecessors, and cases of art made outside any tradition; functional definitions face art that is not intended to afford aesthetic experience; and cluster accounts are criticized as too permissive or as not really definitions. Weitz's paper is dated 1956, Duchamp's Fountain to 1917, and the relevant IEP coverage appears under an Aesthetics or Definition of Art entry rather than under any single fixed title.
misreadings: Defining art is not merely a matter of listing beautiful or well-made things, since much modern art is neither, and beauty is neither necessary nor sufficient for arthood. Weitz's anti-essentialism is not the claim that anything is art, but that art cannot be captured by fixed necessary and sufficient conditions. And relational definitions do not say art has no perceptible features, only that arthood is fixed by relations to a practice rather than by those features, so treating the definition of art as identifying beautiful objects, as implying anything goes, or as denying artworks have qualities, misreads the problem.
origin: The central problem of aesthetics of stating what makes something a work of art, from the classical mimetic, expression, and formalist theories through Weitz's 1956 anti-essentialism to the institutional, historical, and cluster definitions.
